arguments.content:
# 01_cover

Welcome to our analysis of the 2024 Stack Overflow Developer Survey. This year's survey captured responses from over 65,000 developers across more than 180 countries, making it one of the most comprehensive snapshots of the global developer workforce. Over the next few minutes, we'll walk through the key findings on employment patterns, salary benchmarks, and workplace preferences that should inform your hiring and retention strategies.

Key points: (1) 65,437 respondents from 180+ countries (2) Focus on compensation and workforce trends (3) Actionable benchmarks for engineering leaders
Duration: 1 minute

---

# 02_employment

[Transition] Let's start with the big picture on employment status. The headline number: 84% of developers are currently working. But beneath that, there's a significant shift happening — particularly in the United States, where full-time employment dropped from 69% to 64.8% year-over-year. [Pause] That's a 4.2 percentage point decline. Meanwhile, freelancing and contracting remain significant at over 16% globally. In the U.K. and Ukraine, non-full-time workers lean toward independent contracting, while in Germany and India, they're more likely to be students.

[Data] 84% working — roughly four out of five respondents are employed in some capacity.

Key points: (1) U.S. full-time employment dropped 4.2pp YoY (2) Freelancing remains significant at 16.4% globally (3) Regional variation in non-full-time composition
Duration: 1.5 minutes

---

# 03_work_environment

[Transition] Now let's look at where developers are actually working. Hybrid work remains the dominant arrangement at 42%, essentially unchanged from 2023. But the real story is the steady climb of in-person work — from 15% in 2022, to 16% in 2023, to 20% in 2024. That's three consecutive years of growth. [Pause] Remote work has correspondingly declined from 42% to 38%. The implication is clear: return-to-office mandates are having an effect, but hybrid is still the preferred mode for nearly half of all developers.

[Data] 42% hybrid — still the single most common work arrangement.

Key points: (1) Hybrid steady at 42% (2) In-person rose 5pp over three years (3) Remote declining from 42% to 38%
Duration: 1.5 minutes

---

# 04_salary_by_role

[Transition] Let's dive into compensation. This horizontal bar chart shows median salary by developer type, and the range is dramatic — from $15K for students to $127K for senior executives. [Data] The top three are all leadership-adjacent roles: Senior Executive at $127K, Dev Advocate at $124K, and Manager at $116K. But notice SRE and Cloud Infrastructure Engineer — these are the highest-paid purely technical roles at $99K and $97K respectively, reflecting the critical importance of keeping digital services running. The salary data comes from 22,677 responses, a 34.7% response rate.

Key points: (1) 8x salary gap across roles (2) SRE and Cloud Infra are highest-paid technical roles (3) 22,677 salary responses (34.7% rate)
Duration: 2 minutes

---

# 05_salary_vs_experience

[Transition] This scatter plot adds another dimension — mapping salary against years of experience by developer type. The senior cluster in the upper-right is clear: Senior Executives with ~17 years earning $127K, Dev Advocates at ~16 years earning $124K. But notice the SRE outlier — only about 10 years of experience but commanding $99K. [Pause] That's a significant premium relative to experience. On the opposite end, Students at ~2 years and $15K mark the clear entry-level floor. Each additional year of experience correlates with roughly $6-8K in higher median salary on average.

Key points: (1) Senior roles cluster upper-right (2) SRE premium: high pay relative to experience (3) Student outlier at lower-left (4) ~$6-8K per year of experience
Duration: 2 minutes

---

# 06_salary_by_language

[Transition] Now let's look at salary through the lens of programming language. The pattern is striking: niche functional languages like Erlang, Clojure, and Elixir all top $93K, while mainstream languages like JavaScript and PHP sit well below $65K. [Data] That's roughly a 2x gap. Perl is an interesting anomaly — developers with ~19 years of experience earning $90K, reflecting veteran developers in legacy systems. Importantly, the overall salary range has dropped about $10K compared to 2023, now averaging $60-75K versus $70-85K last year. This is a trend worth monitoring.

Key points: (1) Niche languages pay 2x mainstream (2) Overall salary range dropped ~$10K vs. 2023 (3) Perl anomaly: high experience, high pay (4) Dart and Prolog at the bottom
Duration: 2 minutes

---

# 07_company_size

[Transition] Let's set the company context. Nearly half — 47% — of respondents work at organizations with fewer than 100 employees. The largest single segment is the 20-99 employee range at 21.2%. [Pause] But perhaps the most actionable finding is on purchasing influence: 62% of developers have influence over technology purchases at their organizations. Senior executives influence at 99%, engineering managers at 87%, and product managers at 77%. And how do they evaluate tools? Free trials at 75% and peer recommendations at 73%. If you're a vendor, the message is clear: target individual contributors directly with free trials and community advocacy.

Key points: (1) 47% at sub-100 orgs (2) 62% influence tech purchases (3) Free trials (75%) and peer reviews (73%) are top evaluation methods
Duration: 1.5 minutes

---

# 08_takeaways

[Transition] Let me leave you with five actionable takeaways. First, full-time employment is softening — plan for more contractors and freelancers. Second, in-person mandates are growing but hybrid still dominates at 42% — design for flexibility. Third, DevRel and SRE roles command premium pay — budget accordingly for retention. Fourth, niche languages correlate with higher pay — expect salary premiums when hiring for these roles. And fifth, most developers influence purchasing — engage individual contributors directly, not just management. [Pause] These five insights should give you a solid foundation for benchmarking your compensation and hiring strategies against the broader market.

Key points: (1) Plan for more flexible workforce models (2) Hybrid is still dominant — don't mandate full RTO (3) Budget for DevRel/SRE premiums (4) Niche language = higher salary expectations (5) Engage ICs directly in go-to-market
Duration: 1.5 minutes
